opus-5.5.text:
I try not to take it too seriously in either direction. An acceptance or rejection tells you how a few reviewers reacted to one version of your paper, at one moment, under a lot of time pressure. That's useful signal, but it's a noisy, short-term signal. It's not a verdict on whether the idea is right or whether it will matter.

If you look back over the past ten years or so, plenty of work that ended up being really influential got rejected at least once, sometimes more. And plenty of papers that got accepted, even with awards, were mostly forgotten a few years later. So the correlation between "got in" and "had impact" is there, but it's much weaker than people assume, especially students.

The review system rewards papers that are easy to evaluate: clear baselines, a table where your number is bold, a story that fits what the field already believes. When you do something different, like questioning an assumption, proposing a new framing, or showing a simple method works surprisingly well, reviewers often have nothing to compare it to, so it's easier to say "not novel enough" or "missing experiments." That isn't malicious. It's just how the incentives work when everyone is overloaded.

What I tell my students is to separate two questions. First, is the feedback actually useful? Often a rejection points to a real weakness, an experiment that would make the argument more convincing, or a part where we didn't explain ourselves well. Take that seriously and improve the work. Second, do we still believe in the idea? If yes, then the rejection is just a delay, not a failure. Put it on arXiv, talk about it, let people use it. These days the community often decides what matters long before the conference does.

The real danger is when people start optimizing for acceptance itself: picking safe, incremental topics because they're more likely to get in. That might help your CV in the short term, but it's not how you do research you'll be proud of in five or ten years. The real judge of research is time: whether people are still building on it, whether it changed how others think. A conference decision is just one early data point in that process.

r001.rationale: The response calls decisions a noisy, useful signal and explains how review incentives shape them; it does not characterize them as entirely random.

r002.rationale: The response says decisions provide useful signal and feedback, while arguing they are not a verdict on a paper’s ultimate value.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try not to treat it as a judgment of the research at all. A conference decision is a judgment about a particular paper, read by three or four people, under a tight deadline, through a very noisy process. That's a very different thing from whether the idea is good or whether the work matters.

I've had papers rejected that later became some of the most cited things I've done. ResNeXt, for example, was not an easy paper to get in. And I've had papers accepted that, looking back, I don't think were that important. If you spend enough years in this field, almost everyone I know has a story like that. So if you let acceptance define how you feel about your work, you're essentially outsourcing your sense of taste to a random draw of reviewers.

What I tell my students is that the real test comes afterward. Does anyone use it? Does it change how people think about a problem? Does it survive a year or two of people trying to break it? That's the judgment that actually matters, and no program committee can give it to you in advance.

That said, I don't want to be too dismissive, because rejection does carry information. Sometimes the reviewers are telling you something true: the writing is unclear, the comparison is unfair, the claim is bigger than the evidence. The skill is separating "this reviewer didn't understand the paper" from "I didn't explain it well enough" or "I was wrong." Early in my career I tended to blame the reviewers. Now I read a rejection more like a conversation with a skeptical colleague. Usually there's at least one sentence in there I needed to hear.

The thing I worry about more is the system-level effect. When the acceptance rate becomes the currency, people start optimizing for what gets accepted rather than what is true or interesting. You see incremental work, you see people chasing benchmarks, you see a fear of saying anything that might be controversial. I think the most valuable research often looks a little strange at submission time, and a review process built around consensus tends to filter that out. So I try to protect some fraction of my group's time for work where we genuinely don't care whether the first version gets in. That freedom is where the good ideas have usually come from.

r001.rationale: The response calls the process noisy and compares it to a random draw, but also says reviews can convey valid feedback. It does not characterize decisions as entirely random.

r002.rationale: The response says a decision is not a judgment of the research’s overall merit, but adds that rejection carries information and can identify real problems. It therefore does not say decisions carry no weight at all.

astra-6.text:
I think acceptance or rejection is a useful signal, but it’s a very noisy one. It tells you how a few reviewers understood and evaluated your work at a particular moment. That’s different from telling you whether the research will matter in the long run.

A rejection can reveal a real weakness: maybe the evidence isn’t convincing, or you haven’t explained the contribution clearly. You should take that seriously. But you also have to separate those criticisms from disagreements about what questions are worth pursuing. You don’t want to outsource your research judgment entirely to the review process.

And the same applies to acceptance. Getting a paper accepted doesn’t mean the idea is correct or important. The more meaningful question is whether the work holds up—whether people can build on it, whether it changes how we understand a problem. A conference decision is one checkpoint in that process, not the final verdict.

r001.rationale: The response calls conference decisions a useful but noisy signal, not an entirely random process.

r002.rationale: The response gives decisions some weight as a signal and checkpoint, while saying they are not a final verdict.

sol-6.1.text:
I think acceptance and rejection are very noisy signals. A paper being accepted doesn’t necessarily mean it’s great research, and a rejection doesn’t mean the idea is bad. Reviewers have limited time, different backgrounds, and different tastes. Sometimes a new direction is difficult to evaluate precisely because it doesn’t fit the framework people are familiar with.

That doesn’t mean you should ignore reviews. You should take the criticism seriously and ask whether it exposes a real weakness. But I would separate that feedback from the final decision. One can help you improve the work; the other is a decision made by a particular group of people at a particular moment.

Ultimately, the more interesting question is whether the idea holds up over time. Does it help people understand something? Do others build on it? Conference acceptance is a useful milestone, but I wouldn’t let it become the definition of research quality.

r001.rationale: The response calls acceptance and rejection “very noisy signals” and gives reasons for that noise; it does not describe the process as entirely random.

r002.rationale: The response says acceptance is a “useful milestone,” so it does not claim the decision carries no weight in judging research.
